lab_title: Retrograde Motion: Solving the Puzzle of Mars's Backward Loop
top_level_objectives: Recognize and describe the apparent retrograde motion of Mars as observed from Earth's surface against background stars.
Explain why the geocentric model required epicycles to account for retrograde motion, and identify the limitations of that explanation.
Demonstrate how the heliocentric model naturally produces apparent retrograde motion through the relative orbital speeds of Earth and Mars.
Connect the retrograde phenomenon to an everyday analogy involving relative motion between two moving objects.
Compare the retrograde behavior of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and relate the differences to their distances from the Sun.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 1 – Setting the Stage: Mars in the Night Sky
scenes.brief_purpose: Orient students to the phenomenon by showing Mars as a naked-eye observer would see it: a reddish point of light drifting slowly eastward among the background constellations over many weeks. This establishes the 'normal' eastward drift before the anomaly is introduced.
key_visuals: A wide, immersive AR night-sky dome populated with recognizable constellations (e.g., Scorpius, Ophiuchus) rendered as faint star patterns
Mars displayed as a bright, distinctly reddish point of light positioned against the star field
A faint dotted trail showing Mars's eastward path over the previous several weeks
A date counter in the corner advancing night by night as the student scrubs through time
student_actions: Use a time-scrub slider to advance the simulation night by night and watch Mars creep eastward relative to background stars
Tap Mars to reveal a label confirming its identity and current position relative to a named constellation
Answer a brief embedded check: 'In which direction is Mars currently moving relative to the background stars?'

scenes.scene_name: Scene 2 – The Anomaly: Mars Reverses Course
scenes.brief_purpose: Confront students with the retrograde puzzle by letting them witness Mars slow, stop, reverse westward in a looping arc, then resume eastward motion — the full retrograde episode compressed into an interactive time-lapse.
key_visuals: The same night-sky dome from Scene 1, now spanning a ~6-month window centered on opposition
Mars's complete retrograde loop traced as a glowing arc against the star field, forming a visible westward excursion and then a return
Highlight markers at three key moments: first stationary point (Mars stops), midpoint of retrograde (Mars farthest west), and second stationary point (Mars resumes east)
A persistent trail that draws itself in real time as the student advances the date
student_actions: Scrub through the 6-month window and observe the full loop form on the sky
Tap each of the three highlight markers to read a short label explaining what is happening at that moment (e.g., 'First Stationary Point — Mars appears to pause')
Sketch or trace the loop shape using a simple AR drawing tool overlaid on the star field, then compare their trace to the actual path

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3 – The Geocentric Attempt: Epicycles to the Rescue?
scenes.brief_purpose: Present the historical geocentric explanation — the epicycle — so students appreciate both its ingenuity and its awkwardness. A geocentric orrery shows Earth at the center with Mars riding a small circle (epicycle) on a larger circle (deferent), reproducing the loop but at the cost of added complexity.
key_visuals: A compact AR orrery model floating at table height with Earth fixed at the center, surrounded by a large circular deferent ring for Mars
A smaller epicycle circle attached to a point on the deferent, with a Mars figure riding the epicycle
Animated motion showing Mars tracing its looping path as the epicycle carries it around
A split inset panel showing the resulting sky-path loop matching what was seen in Scene 2, connecting the mechanism to the observation
student_actions: Press a Play button to animate the geocentric model and watch how the epicycle generates the retrograde loop
Use a pinch gesture to slow or speed up the animation to inspect the relationship between Mars's position on the epicycle and the direction of its apparent sky motion
Respond to a prompt: 'Does this model successfully reproduce the loop? What feels unsatisfying or arbitrary about the explanation?' — a free-response text or voice note recorded for reflection

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4 – The Heliocentric View: Stepping Outside the Solar System
scenes.brief_purpose: Transport students to an overhead 'god's-eye' perspective of the solar system, showing the Sun at the center with Earth and Mars both orbiting in the same direction. This view reveals the true geometry that produces the apparent loop.
key_visuals: A top-down AR solar system model with the Sun at center, Earth's orbit as a smaller ellipse, and Mars's orbit as a larger ellipse, both labeled with orbital period data
Animated Earth and Mars figures moving along their orbits at their correct relative speeds, with Earth visibly faster than Mars
A line-of-sight ray extending from Earth through Mars outward to a distant star-background ring, showing the direction Earth's observers would look to see Mars
The line-of-sight ray's intersection with the background ring highlighted, updating in real time to trace the retrograde loop on the background ring as Earth overtakes Mars
student_actions: Press Play to animate both planets and watch the line-of-sight trace the retrograde loop on the background ring
Pause the animation at the point of closest approach (opposition) and rotate around the model using AR head or hand movement to inspect the geometry from multiple angles
Tap Earth and Mars separately to see their orbital speeds displayed (Earth ~29.8 km/s, Mars ~24.1 km/s) and read the explanation of why Earth overtakes Mars

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5 – The Passing-Car Analogy: Making It Intuitive
scenes.brief_purpose: Anchor the abstract orbital geometry to a concrete everyday experience by presenting the passing-car analogy, helping students internalize why a faster inner orbit produces an apparent backward shift of the slower outer object.
key_visuals: An AR highway scene rendered at ground level showing two parallel lanes: a faster car (labeled 'Earth') in the inner lane and a slower car (labeled 'Mars') in the outer lane
Background scenery (trees, distant hills) serving as the 'background stars'
A highlighted line of sight from the Earth-car to the Mars-car extending to the background, with a marker showing where it intersects the background
A split-screen or overlay connecting the highway scene back to the heliocentric orbital diagram from Scene 4
student_actions: Trigger the animation and watch the Mars-car appear to drift backward relative to the background scenery as the Earth-car overtakes it, even though both cars move forward
Drag a slider to control the speed difference between the two cars and observe how a larger speed difference changes the apparent backward drift
Answer a conceptual check: 'If Earth and Mars traveled at the same orbital speed, would we ever see retrograde motion? Why or why not?'

scenes.scene_name: Scene 6 – Comparing Planets: Mars vs. Jupiter vs. Saturn
scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the concept by showing that all outer planets exhibit retrograde motion but that the effect diminishes with distance from the Sun, because the speed difference and parallax effect both decrease as the outer planet's orbit grows larger.
key_visuals: A scaled-down top-down solar system showing orbits of Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn simultaneously, with each outer planet highlighted in a distinct color

Side-by-side retrograde loop traces for all three outer planets displayed on a shared star-background ring, visually demonstrating that Mars's loop is the most dramatic and Saturn's is the most subtle
Data callout bubbles showing approximate retrograde duration and angular loop size for each planet (Mars ~72 days / ~15°, Jupiter ~120 days / ~10°, Saturn ~138 days / ~7°)
Speed and distance comparison bars displayed alongside each planet's orbit
student_actions: Select each planet using AR tap to isolate its retrograde animation and inspect its loop shape against the background ring
Arrange the three loop traces in order from largest to smallest by dragging them into a ranking panel, then confirm their ranking

Read and interact with an embedded explanation connecting loop size to the relative speed difference and orbital distance, with a final summary prompt asking students to state the relationship in their own words

scenes.scene_name: Scene 7 – Synthesis: Geocentric vs. Heliocentric Side-by-Side
scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate understanding by presenting both models simultaneously so students can directly compare their elegance and explanatory power, reinforcing why the heliocentric model displaced the geocentric model for this phenomenon.
key_visuals: A split AR workspace: the geocentric epicycle orrery on the left and the heliocentric orbital diagram on the right, both animated simultaneously and synchronized to the same date window
Both models generating the same retrograde sky loop, displayed as a shared sky-trail panel above both orreries
Visual complexity indicators — the geocentric side shows multiple overlapping circles while the heliocentric side shows two clean ellipses
Historical portraits or name labels of Ptolemy and Copernicus anchored near their respective models
student_actions: Play both animations simultaneously and observe that both reproduce the loop, then tap a 'Complexity Meter' button that counts the number of geometric elements each model requires
Use a reflection prompt to record a short voice or text note: 'Which model do you find more satisfying, and what scientific principle supports preferring the simpler explanation?'

Complete a final three-question multiple-choice quiz embedded in the scene covering (1) the cause of retrograde motion, (2) the role of relative orbital speed, and (3) the comparison across outer planets — receiving immediate feedback and a summary of key takeaways
